title: Site Reliability Engineering
subtitle: Keep services dependable by measuring user outcomes, improving observability, and learning from incidents.
summary: Keep services dependable by measuring user outcomes, improving observability, and learning from incidents.
audience: Learners building practical computer engineering skills

units.title: 1. Service operations and reliability basics
units.description: Service boundaries, user journeys, availability, latency, dependencies, and operational ownership.

lessons.title: Define a service around user journeys
lessons.summary: Define a service around user journeys. Learn the key idea, then apply it to a realistic system decision.
notes: A service is a user-facing capability that may depend on several components and teams. A user journey describes the steps that create value, such as signing in and viewing a course. Reliability should be measured against those outcomes, not only whether a process is running.

Draw the service boundary around what the team owns and list critical dependencies. A page may load while sign-in or payment fails, so define which journeys matter and how each can be observed. Clear ownership helps responders know who can make a decision during an incident.

quiz.question: The page loads but users cannot complete checkout. Is the service reliable?
options: No; a key user journey is failing even if one component responds.
Yes; any successful HTTP response proves reliability.
Assume the system behavior without checking it.
quiz.explanation: No; a key user journey is failing even if one component responds. Confirm it with relevant evidence and state any limits.

lessons.title: Map dependencies and operational ownership
lessons.summary: Map dependencies and operational ownership. Learn the key idea, then apply it to a realistic system decision.
notes: Failure modes describe ways a component or dependency can fail and the effect on users. Capacity limits, configuration mistakes, unavailable dependencies, and bad releases create different symptoms. Toil is repetitive operational work that consumes time without improving the service permanently.

Before automating toil, understand the task and its failure conditions. Add guardrails, logs, and an owner. Reliability work is most effective when teams know who responds, which dependencies matter, and what routine work could be safely removed.

units.title: 2. SLIs, SLOs, and error budgets
units.description: Choose useful indicators, define objectives, understand error budgets, and use reliability goals to guide decisions.

lessons.title: Choose a measurable service indicator
lessons.summary: Choose a measurable service indicator. Learn the key idea, then apply it to a realistic system decision.
notes: A service level indicator (SLI) measures a user-relevant behavior, such as successful requests or latency. Define the event, eligible population, data source, and measurement window. A useful SLI makes the service experience measurable rather than simply counting infrastructure activity.

Choose a metric that reflects the promise to users. Averages can hide a slow tail, and server CPU can look normal while requests fail. Check distributions and failure rates and ensure the measurement can be explained and reproduced.

quiz.question: What makes an SLI useful?
options: It measures a clearly defined user-relevant outcome over a stated window.
It counts any system metric that is easy to collect.
Assume the system behavior without checking it.
quiz.explanation: It measures a clearly defined user-relevant outcome over a stated window. Confirm it with relevant evidence and state any limits.

practice.title: SLIs, SLOs, and error budgets
practice.prompt: Average latency hides very slow requests. What can reveal the tail?
options: Choose the fastest action without checking impact.
A high latency percentile and the distribution.
Only the mean.
practice.explanation: A high latency percentile and the distribution. This keeps the work scoped and reviewable.

lessons.title: Set an objective and use its error budget
lessons.summary: Set an objective and use its error budget. Learn the key idea, then apply it to a realistic system decision.
notes: A service level objective (SLO) sets a target for an SLI over a defined window. An error budget represents the unreliability the target allows during that window. Teams can use it to balance release speed and reliability work based on observed service behavior.

An SLO is not a guarantee. Agree on what happens when the budget is being spent quickly, and use that policy consistently. If the indicator, target, or window is vague, a team cannot compare results or make a clear release decision.

units.title: 3. Observability and monitoring
units.description: Metrics, logs, traces, alert quality, dashboards, and symptom-focused monitoring.

lessons.title: Use metrics, logs, and traces together
lessons.summary: Use metrics, logs, and traces together. Learn the key idea, then apply it to a realistic system decision.
notes: Metrics summarize numeric behavior, logs record events, and traces connect work across services for a request. Together, they can narrow a user symptom into a likely failing component. Correlation identifiers and consistent timestamps make it easier to follow events across systems.

Telemetry should be chosen for a question and designed to avoid exposing credentials or unnecessary personal information. Start from a user-visible symptom, then use metrics to see the pattern, traces to locate a path, and logs to inspect relevant events.

quiz.question: Which telemetry can connect one request across multiple services?
options: A distributed trace with spans from the relevant services.
A disk capacity metric alone.
Assume the system behavior without checking it.
quiz.explanation: A distributed trace with spans from the relevant services. Confirm it with relevant evidence and state any limits.

options: Choose the fastest action without checking impact.

practice.explanation: A structured log correlated by request or transaction identifier. This keeps the work scoped and reviewable.

lessons.title: Design alerts that help someone act
lessons.summary: Design alerts that help someone act. Learn the key idea, then apply it to a realistic system decision.
notes: An alert should indicate an actionable risk, have an owner, and provide a useful first step. Symptom-based alerts focus on user impact; diagnostic signals help explain causes. Dashboards should answer a defined operational question rather than display every available metric.

Noisy alerts train responders to ignore them. Review false positives and missed incidents, tune thresholds against objectives, and include a runbook or escalation path. Page only when urgent action is needed; route lower-priority signals to an appropriate review queue.

units.title: 4. Incident response and learning
units.description: Incident roles, communication, mitigation, blameless review, and turning findings into durable improvements.

lessons.title: Stabilize service and communicate during an incident
lessons.summary: Stabilize service and communicate during an incident. Learn the key idea, then apply it to a realistic system decision.
notes: An incident is an unexpected event that threatens service or data. Responders establish roles, assess impact, mitigate the problem, and communicate updates. A shared timeline records observations and actions so people can coordinate without relying on memory.

During an incident, reducing user impact can be more important than identifying the root cause immediately. If a recent change is strongly correlated with a failure, a reversible rollback may be the right mitigation while investigation continues. Record why the decision was made.

quiz.question: During an outage, a recent change correlates with failures but root cause is unknown. What is reasonable?
options: Mitigate user impact, such as rolling back, while investigation continues.
Wait for certainty before taking any action.
Assume the system behavior without checking it.
quiz.explanation: Mitigate user impact, such as rolling back, while investigation continues. Confirm it with relevant evidence and state any limits.

practice.title: Incident response and learning
practice.prompt: What makes an incident follow-up useful?
options: Choose the fastest action without checking impact.
A specific owner and a change whose effect can be verified.
A general reminder to be more careful.
practice.explanation: A specific owner and a change whose effect can be verified. This keeps the work scoped and reviewable.

lessons.title: Turn incident evidence into owned improvements
lessons.summary: Turn incident evidence into owned improvements. Learn the key idea, then apply it to a realistic system decision.
notes: A post-incident review examines what happened, how the system behaved, and which changes could reduce future impact. Blameless review means looking for conditions and incentives that shaped actions rather than blaming an individual. Findings should be specific, prioritized, and owned.

“Be more careful” is not a reliable control. Prefer changes such as a missing alert, a safer default, an automated check, or a tested rollback. Track whether the change happened and whether it improved the signal or reduced the failure path.

units.title: 5. Automation, capacity, and resilience
units.description: Automate one repetitive task, load-test a sample service, plan capacity, and write a runbook and reliability review.

lessons.title: Automate toil with safe guardrails
lessons.summary: Automate toil with safe guardrails. Learn the key idea, then apply it to a realistic system decision.
notes: Resilience combines design and operational preparation for failures. Timeouts, bounded retries, capacity planning, redundancy, and graceful degradation can reduce impact when dependencies slow or disappear. Each control has tradeoffs; retries without limits can amplify load during an outage.

Practice failure scenarios safely and measure recovery. Load tests should have defined scope and limits, especially when a shared service is involved. Backups, failover, and rollback need regular exercises; untested recovery steps are assumptions, not demonstrated capability.

quiz.question: Why should retries be bounded and use backoff?
options: To avoid adding load to a dependency that is already failing.
To make each request retry forever at maximum speed.
Assume the system behavior without checking it.
quiz.explanation: To avoid adding load to a dependency that is already failing. Confirm it with relevant evidence and state any limits.

practice.title: Automation, capacity, and resilience
practice.prompt: What demonstrates a recovery plan works?
options: Choose the fastest action without checking impact.
A documented restore or failover exercise with results and gaps.
A diagram labeled “high availability.”
practice.explanation: A documented restore or failover exercise with results and gaps. This keeps the work scoped and reviewable.

lessons.title: Plan capacity, failure handling, and recovery
lessons.summary: Plan capacity, failure handling, and recovery. Learn the key idea, then apply it to a realistic system decision.
notes: A reliability review connects user journeys to SLIs, SLOs, alerts, dependencies, and mitigation steps. State what is in scope and what evidence supports the reliability claim. A small service can still benefit from a clear owner, health signals, and an incident plan.

For a capstone, define a user outcome, calculate an objective from sample data, investigate a simulated incident, and recommend a measurable follow-up. Explain limitations and avoid claiming that a short exercise proves production readiness.
